events.summary: Curated by Harriet Tubman Center for Expanded Curatorial Practice at MLK School and Lisa Jarrett Drawing from the Museum’s collection, this exhibition is co-curated by Lisa Jarrett, an artist, educator, and curator, and the Harriet Tubman Center for Expanded Curatorial Practice at MLK Elementary— a group of 4th and 5th grade curators from KSMoCA. Working from a conversation with notable curators Dr. Lowery Stokes Sims and Dr. Leslie King Hammond, the exhibition engages PAM’s collection in new dialogues shaped by emerging curatorial voices and multigenerational knowledge. From theme and concept development, through work selection, and installation, this community curators project highlights the collaborative nature of curatorial practice and museum work. Harriet Tubman Center for Expanded Curatorial Practice at MLK School \(HTC\) is a KSMoCA project. Students participate directly in shaping exhibitions, positioning them as contributors to the museum, and engaging them as researchers, writers, planners, and curators. Through workshops and field trips, students collaborate with artists, visiting curators, and mentors from Portland State University’s College of the Arts. They research how exhibitions are developed, how artworks are interpreted, and how institutional decisions shape public understanding. Expanded curatorial practice includes visual art, writing, performance, research, publishing, and social practice. Co-founded by Lisa Jarrett and Harrell Fletcher, the project began in 2018 at Harriet Tubman Middle School and continues in its current iteration at Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. Elementary School.
events.title: Harriet Tubman Center Museum

events.summary: Inspired by Katherine Ace’s 9 Portraits as the foundational starting point for the exhibition, Nine Women Artists will feature the work of the artists shown in Ace’s portrait painting. All mature artists in their careers and with a significant presence in the Northwest, their work reveals a diverse expression of artistic styles from representation to abstraction. There are rich details in the painting. Most notably on the left hangs Henri Fantin-Latour’s A Studio at Les Batignolles, 1870 \(Musée d’Orsay\). In this painting is a formal gathering of male artists. In response to this painting, Katherine asked her subjects to dress in their studio/work clothes as counterpoint, all marked in their characteristic poses. Other Portland women artists are recognized here through their paintings—a small Sally Haley still life hangs in the background, as well as an Amanda Snyder painting behind Phyllis Yes. And to the far right, we have a glimpse of Lucinda Parker’s very large work. Postcards and newspapers scattered on the floor are the exhibition announcements and reviews highlighting the artists’ works. An epic portrait featuring nine women artists of the Northwest, Ace responded to the lack of self-portraits by women artists in history. From left, the artists are: Laura Ross-Paul, Katherine’s self-portrait seated with phone, Mary Josephson, Judy Cooke, Phyllis Yes, Sharon Bronzan, Shu-Ju Wang, Lucinda Parker, and Sherrie Wolf. All are women artists who have made long careers in Portland. As Ace notes about these women, “They have tenacity, have lived through sexist decades, told they couldn’t really be artists—only fit for sleeping with the professor, expected to subvert themselves to male artist machismo.”
events.title: Nine Women Artists

events.summary: Get moving with a beginner Tai Chi class by Many Roads Martial Arts Center on Sundays. 10:30 – 11:30 AM | Sundays, May 3 – October 25, 2026 Many Roads Martial Arts Center is offering an introductory Tai Chi class at Lan Su on Sundays at 10:30AM. This class will introduce the fundamental principles of Tai Chi Chaun \(or Taijiquan\) using the Yang Style 24 Posture Form. We will work on posture and body alignment alongside principles of movement and meditation. We will also discuss how Tai Chi blends health, meditation, and martial application. This class is suitable for all levels but will be particularly helpful for beginners of all ages. Get Admission Meet the Instructors: Many Roads Martial Arts Center Jenny Lohr, Owner/Instructor Jenny has been practicing Shaolin Kung Fu and Tai Chi since 2005. As the owner of Many Roads Martial Arts Center, her focus is nurturing a supportive and safe learning environment while challenging everyone to keep growing and improving. Jenny loves the physical and mental challenges of martial arts and is very excited to share them with the students and instructors at the center. Jay Twitchell, Instructor Jay has studied various martial arts systems including boxing, wrestling, judo, karate, taekwondo, aikido, hopkido, kumdo, and muay thai kick boxing since he was 10. In other words, he has been used as a punching bag for over 30 years by masters and lifelong practitioners of these systems. His lifetime of experience getting kicked, punched, choked, kneed, elbowed, and thrown are invaluable in teaching others how not to be. Balancing his martial studies, Jay has 20 years of experience as a massage therapist and movement specialist, offering him a deep knowledge of the human body and healthy practice. Myk Olsen, Instructor Myk has been a Tai Chi Chuan practitioner since 1997 and has been teaching since 2013. His primary teachers were Gao Jamin and Yu Shaowen. Over the years, Myk has learned a multitude of forms in Yang, Chen, Wu, and Sun styles—both open-hand and weapons \(straight sword, broadsword, staff, spear, cane, deerhorn knives, and daggers\). While he used to compete in both forms and Push-Hands, Myk now focuses more time on teaching. His teaching style is student-centered and is focused on achieving a balance between the meditative and martial aspects of the forms. Myk also teaches a Tai Chi class specifically geared toward those with mobility and balance issues on Sunday afternoon. Joel, Instructor A lifetime student of martial arts, Joel has been training Shaolin Kung Fu and Tai Chi since 1999 and teaching since 2009. His teaching goal is to provide tools to improve every student’s physical, mental, and emotional health in a supportive, encouraging learning environment. Joel’s primary teaching focus is Chen Tai Chi as taught by Master George Xu \(Xu Guo Ming\). He also teaches our black belt Shaolin curriculum, Yang style Tai Chi, and 5 Element Qi Gong. Learn more Or follow them on social media: Facebook | Instagram Parking & Directions Free Lan Su Parking There is free first come, first served parking in our sister lot next to the garden at 424 NW Third Avenue. Art that focuses on fears, phobias, or disquieting themes. Settings or characters or creatures that are dark, born from night, or upsetting to see. Images that capture the fun and nostalgia of playing in a scary space through a safe lens, reminiscent of horror movies and Halloweens past. Come in for a thrill and a chill, find a new piece to haunt your home, and enjoy beautiful works of art perfect for those who are strange and unusual. Alberta Street Gallery is a friendly and vibrant cooperative gallery of 30 local artists in the heart of the Alberta Arts District in Northeast Portland. In addition to our members’ art, we mount monthly shows that begin on the “Last Thursday” of every month. Our front windows feature new work by two of our member artists, and we curate group shows in Lavaun's Community Gallery, a special exhibition space inside the gallery named for and made possible by gallery member Lavaun Benavidez Heaster, a legally blind collage artist who died in 2020.

events.summary: Fat Over Lean is a free art exhibition celebrating fat bodies, fat artists, and the many ways fatness intersects with queerness, disability, identity, and belonging. Curated by Portland artist Michelle Jackson, the exhibition brings together artwork by over 30 fat artists from across the Pacific Northwest, including painting, photography, fiber, ceramics, mixed media, and more. Created in response to the lack of positive and nuanced representation of fat bodies in the arts, Fat Over Lean is about making space for people whose bodies and experiences are too often left out of galleries. The exhibition will also feature free community events and creative programming throughout October. See works by Alexis Barnes, Ana Mai Luckett, Aurora Owen, Cherie Savoie Tintary, Eko Salamanca, Fi Bu, Garrett Stache, Heather Lobitz, Heather Weitman, Jessie Wu, Jo MahnkeVanHuss, Johnny Sheckler, JUUPI, KT Kusmaul / Body Home Fat Dance, Laura Grae Miller, Lyzz Stewart, M. V. Moran, Madison Flickinger, McKinley Johnson, Michelle Jackson, Morgan Wilhelm, Nat & Jess Breece, Richelle Fullerton, Roselynn La Jeunesse, Ruby Webb, Shaun Crabb, Shayla Smith, Shelby Fercik, Miss Joomina, Sossity Chiricuzio, Stevie Rosman-Hyde, Tarina Bagua, and Uwin Hakan. Join us for these upcoming events: Opening Reception: Saturday, October 3rd, 3- 8 p.m. Why Don't I Draw Myself Fat? Saturday, October 24th from 6 - 7:30 pm. A miniature Art Show and Telltale night of storytelling and taking up space in community hosted by Telltale Presents Closing Reception/Halloween Party: Saturday, October 31st, 7 - 9 pm. About Fat Over Lean Fat Over Lean is a project that aims to lower barriers to the arts for fat, queer, and disabled people by creating opportunities to share their work within the greater Portland, Oregon, and southern Washington communities. Artists were not charged a fee to apply for this show, and they will not pay a commission on artwork sold during the exhibition, aside from standard transaction fees. We believe artists should be able to share their work without having to navigate unnecessary financial barriers. By supporting fat artists, creators, and educators, Fat Over Lean hopes to create more opportunities for growth, visibility, advancement, and connection. This project is about making room: for fat bodies, for queer and disabled voices, for artists who are often asked to take up less space, and for the communities that grow when we get to show up as ourselves. This project was made possible by RACC, Portland Arts & Culture, Fans Only Studio, and Portland Clean Air Committee. Visit Fat Over Lean or Michelle's Instagram for events and gallery hours.

events.summary: We Built You a Garden is the third installment of Metro’s Community Voices project, a multimedia storytelling initiative that invites residents of Metro Affordable Housing Bond-funded communities to explore the meaning of home through photography, writing and collective reflection. Hosted through a summer workshop series at the Strong Empowerment Village in partnership with artists Gwen Hoeffgen and Domenic Toliver, the project centers the experiences of residents with ties to North and Northeast Portland. Through weekly workshops and the use of film photography and creative writing, participants documented places, people and memories that shape their understanding of home, legacy and belonging. Their work considers displacement, resilience and community history, creating a powerful collection of stories that honor the past while imagining what can continue to grow. Ultimately, We Built You a Garden asks what’s been inherited, what’s been built, and what we want to leave growing for the next generation. It speaks to the ongoing impact of displacement in Portland for the Black community, but it also affirms what it took — and continues to take — to nourish, tend and build home. Exhibition and events: Free admission Oct. 9, 5:30pm to 8pm: We Built You a Garden | Exhibition Opening at The BLACK Gallery Join us for the opening of We Built You a Garden, with remarks and refreshments as well as free copies of the project’s publication. Open to public with remarks from Metro, artists, and Don’t Shoot PDX . Oct. 23, 6pm to 8pm: We Built You a Garden | Community Conversation at The BLACK Gallery A conversation about the past, present, and future of Portland through the experiences of the people who live, work, organize, and build here. Artists, activists, community members, youth and Metro come together to consider what we have inherited, what we have built, what is changing, and what we want to leave growing for the next generation. The BLACK Gallery will be open to the public on the following Sundays from 1pm to 4pm during the exhibition’s display: Oct. 11, Oct. 18, Oct. 25 and Nov. 1.

events.summary: Written in 1936, this light-hearted comedy has relevance for today in addressing the main theme of finding one’s own way in today’s complex society, while lightly viewing such topics as distrust of government, domestic terrorism and fear of foreign conflicts. “Grandpa” Vanderhof (Robert Lovitz) once worked in the competitive business world. One day, he realized he was unhappy, so he stopped working. Since then, he spends his days catching and raising snakes, watching graduation ceremonies, visiting old friends, and doing whatever else he wants. His daughter Penny (Marilyn Stacey) writes plays simply because a few years ago a typewriter was delivered to the house by accident. His son-in-law Paul Sycamore (Todd Hermanson) spends hours in the basement making illegal fireworks and playing with erector sets. His granddaughter Essie (Bonnie Auguston) sells candy and has been clumsily attempting ballet for over eight years. His grandson-in-law Ed Carmichael (Aiden Brown) plays the xylophone (or tries to) and accidentally distributes Marxist propaganda. Joining this free-for-all are Rheba (Caren Graham), the household cook; her unemployed boyfriend, Donald (Shaun Hennessy); Essie’s opinionated Russian ballet instructor, Mr. Kolenkhov (Mark Schwahn); Olga (Trisha Todd), a Russian Grand Duchess; Gay Wellington (Adrienne Southard), a heavy-drinking actress; Wilbur C. Henderson (Douglas Hout), a forlorn IRS employee; and Mr. De Pinna (Danny Bruno), a deliveryman who arrived 8 years ago and decided to stay. He now helps with the fireworks and dresses in Roman togas to pose for Penny’s portraits. All is somewhat calm until three men from the government (Christopher Sparks, Dan Weiss, and Erik James) visit to investigate Ed’s flyers. In this crazy mix of characters, there is also Alice (Taylor Jean Grady), Penny and Paul’s other daughter and, apparently, the only “normal” family member. She met Tony Kirby (Noah Matthew Rich) at his dad’s Wall Street investment firm, and they’ve fallen in love. Culture shock and fireworks fly when Mr. Kirby (Jeremy Southard) and Mrs. Kirby (Wendy Martel) come to visit. But the message is clear: “Life’s pretty simple if you just relax,” as Grandpa puts it. You Can’t Take It With You is directed by Don Alder. Set design is by Chris Whitten, lighting design is by Demetri Pavlatos, costume design is by Janelle Sutton, prop design is by Allen R. Phillips, the stage manager is Alex Salem, the assistant stage manager is Nat Weinham, and the producer is Steve Knox.

events.summary: Jesse Preis debuts The Raven, a chamber opera composed for three voices and chamber ensemble from Edgar Allan Poe’s poem of the same name, directed by Melory Mirashrafi. In this opera, the narrator (split into two characters to capture the perspective of the Past and the Current at two different stages in life) deals with the loss of a loved one. These complicated, painful, and even terrifying emotions become personified through the character of the Raven. This work is composed with no specific voice types tied to the characters - anyone able to sing the part can and should sing them. This is a groundbreaking composing technique that unties the binds of gendered characters and allows vocalists to portray a character of any gender that is authentic to them and suits their voice. Preis seeks to expand our understanding of vocal writing to go beyond the gendered conventions of soprano, mezzo-soprano, tenor, and bass-baritone, and posits a world where characters are simply written and performed by a wide variety of voices.
events.title: The Raven

events.summary: Sundays 4:30PM - 5:30PM, Oct 4 - Dec 20 | $10/weekly drop in Need a reset for your busy week ahead? Join us Sunday late afternoons for a welcoming, beginner-friendly yoga class focused on foundational poses, mindful movement, breath awareness, and building confidence on the mat. Whether you’re brand new to yoga or looking to reconnect with the fundamentals, this class is designed to help you build a strong foundation through accessible movement, breath work, and foundational poses. We’ll focus on alignment, balance, flexibility, and body awareness in a welcoming, supportive environment. Beginners are encouraged to join, and those with a regular practice will also benefit from slowing down, refining technique, and deepening their understanding of familiar poses. Options and modifications will be offered throughout class so everyone can move at their own pace. Wear comfortable athletic clothes, bring a yoga mat if possible \(a limited number will be available to borrow\), and please arrive 5–10 minutes before class begins so we can start on time. Classes are led by Wyle O'Neill, from Love Our Practice, whose yoga journey began in high school and later led him to study in Mysore and Goa, India, where he deepened his understanding of yoga’s roots and philosophy. Wyle completed his 200-hour RYT training at Yoga Salt with Tamal Dodge and completed his 500-hour teacher training at Sthira Yoga School in Goa, India. His teaching blends accessible movement, meditation, breathwork through an individual-centered practice to help students feel grounded, present, as well as connected to themselves and community.

events.summary: Glass. Kill. Bluebeard. Imp. is a collection of four short, surreal plays by acclaimed English playwright, Caryl Churchill. Premiering at London's Royal Court Theatre in 2019, these darkly imaginative works weave together myth, fairy tale, and contemporary horror. Moving between collective voices and intimate encounters, Churchill explores violence, power, desire, and the stories we tell to make sense of a fractured world. By turns funny, haunting, and unsettling, the plays invite audiences into a landscape where the familiar becomes strange and ancient myths reveal modern anxieties without explanation or comfort. A girl made of glass. Gods and murders. A serial killer's friends. And a secret in a bottle.​ Four short plays by Caryl Churchill Directed by Samantha Van Der Merwe​October 10th - November 7th 2026

She’s been a featured performer at the Netflix Is a Joke Festival, New York Comedy Festival, and Black Women in Comedy Laff Fest. Check her out on instagram @alexisbradby and alexisbradby.com

events.summary: Adapted from Agatha Christie’s classic mystery, this immersive production brings the psychological tension of the classic tale into immediate, breath-held proximity. Our story takes place inside a remote seaside mansion after a violent storm strands ten guests and their hosts. When an eerie accusation recorded on a gramophone accuses each of them of wrongdoing, the guests confront secrets, guilt, and suspicion. Trapped by weather and circumstance, alliances form and fracture… old grievances surface, and rationality gives way to intense fear as each new death raises the stakes. At ETP’s production, you’ll find yourself sitting with the characters within the house itself, among the bedrooms, the dining room, and narrow passages. Experience the shifting power dynamics and mounting claustrophobia as if you were part of the action. Hear whispered confrontations up close, overhear private confessions, and feel the silence before the next crisis. Though the environment surrounds you, the audience is strictly non-participatory — as a silent witness, a “fly on the wall,” you will never be directly addressed by the characters, nor asked to participate. What to expect in performance: \- Tension-driven mystery with tightly controlled pacing and sudden shocks. \- Strong emphasis on atmosphere: storm sound design, flickering lantern and candlelight, thunder, and selective blackout moments. \- Intense emotional scenes: accusations, breakdowns, moral reckonings, and desperate attempts to find the culprit. \- Minimalist, realistic set dressing that transforms the performance space into a lived-in island mansion, with audience seating integrated into set locations (chairs, benches, window alcoves). \- No audience interaction; observers remain silent and stationary throughout each performance. Content warnings: Multiple onstage deaths and depictions of violence (staged, non-graphic). Mature themes and dialogue — recommended for ages 13+ About Experience Theatre Project: Experience Theatre Project is an innovative, immersive theater company based in Aloha, Oregon. Unlike traditional theaters with rows of seats and a proscenium stage, ETP crafts imaginative and fully surrounding narratives, drawing inspiration from both original and classic stories. Our specialty lies in presenting these tales in an unconventional, unexpected fashion, surrounding audiences in the world of the play, similar to a haunted house or a Disney experience. Limiting audiences to sixty or fewer ensures an intimate and memorable experience. Ticket link: www.experiencetheatreproject.org
events.title: ETP Presents Agatha Christie's And Then There Were None

Code & Coffee is an inclusive, informal co-working session: drink your beverage of choice, bring your laptop, and hang out with your peers! Have engaging conversations, or focus on work or projects. This is a great opportunity to learn from others, share your knowledge, and possibly collaborate on side projects, online courses, or even your day-to-day work.

---- Schedule ----

You're welcome to drop in anytime during the event. We understand that everyone may have external commitments and challenges - join us when you can!

We have informal unscheduled introductions - practice your personal elevator pitch, or take things slower to build your confidence.

---- Venue ----

Fly Chai allow us to informally and freely use their space. If within your budget, we'd appreciate your help to sustain our use of the venue, by purchasing something tasty, whether Chai or otherwise.

Find us at tables with a Code&Coffee sign - or a clump of laptop-users!

Wifi and power outlets are available.
Our meeting area should be accessible - please let us know if not.

---- What to expect ----

Smaller events than you may be used to, with a mixed crowd week-to-week. We expect this is likely due to us meeting weekly, at a less central location.

These may result in what you're looking for:
    A smaller, less intimidating, lower pressure, cozy atmosphere.
    A mix of regular and new faces.
    A simpler schedule - every week, same time, same place - that you can drop into when you like.
    Being closer to you than other events.

events.summary: The Multnomah Arts Center (MAC) presents A Good Universe Next Door – A redacted past, a precarious present, and an uncertain future, a group exhibition curated by Celeste Noche and Melanie Stevens. On view in the Front & Center Galleries from September 18 through October 17, 2026, the exhibition features new work by four regional artists: Amber Capwell, Ebony Frison, Maryanna Hollomon, and Orlando Almanza. An opening reception will be held Saturday, September 19, from 1–3 p.m., and an artist talk will take place Saturday, October 10 at 2 p.m. Stevens and Noche invited the artists to consider how utopia and dystopia manifest in their lives, and how they interpret these experiences. Through sculpture, photography, printmaking, and painting, the artists offer visions of futures shaped by remembrance, resistance, solidarity, creativity, and care. Ebony Frison approaches utopia and dystopia as “conditions that coexist within the same historical moment.” Working with archival research, printmaking, photography, and artist books, Frison examines how Black histories persist despite erasure, describing utopia as “a practice of rememory—an active engagement with ancestral knowledge, community care, and historical reclamation.” Maryanna Hollomon highlights the aftermath of war for children and the global systems that produce displacement. “A utopia cannot be achieved without working in solidarity with those most oppressed,” she writes. Her work asks viewers to consider militarism’s impact and to imagine new forms of resistance and collective care. Amber Capwell creates sculptural works that envision utopian possibilities through Tarot readings for endangered Pacific Northwest flora and fauna. “These sculptures exist as a reminder to care,” they write. Their work incorporates queer and trans identities as part of an ecological futurism that demands “a utopia existing where we are allowed to live and thrive.” Orlando Almanza imagines futures built on safety, connection, and community. “I dream of a place where my people can have picnics next to the river, to rest, to laugh… and the grandmothers can enjoy their old age, sitting in their rocking chairs on their front porch,” he writes. “Sueño con el día que pueda ver a mi familia reunida, en la tierra que nos vio nacer” (I dream that one day my family can be reunited, in the land that birthed us). The Multnomah Arts Center is located at 7688 SW Capitol Hwy, Portland, OR, 97219. It is open Monday – Thursday 9 a.m. to 9:30 p.m., and Friday – Saturday 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. Additional Information: The Multnomah Arts Center is a part of Portland Parks & Recreation. MAC offers programs in a wide range of visual, music, movement, theater, and literary arts at an affordable cost to people of all ages. In addition to this vibrant arts education program, MAC runs a community-based visual arts exhibition program, which includes the MAC Front & Center Galleries. MAC also hosts theatre, music and dance performances, and other special events. The Multnomah Arts Center Association (MACA) is an all-volunteer, 501(c)(3) nonprofit organization that exists to support equity and access to arts education at MAC. MACA provides scholarships, supports community engagements efforts, and provides specialized arts equipment and facility improvements. Their efforts expand opportunities and enhance the experience of students, instructors, and the community at-large. For more information about MAC or MACA, please call 503.823.2787 or visit www.multnomahartscenter.org.
events.title: A Good Universe Next Door

events.summary: Skeletons Out of the Closet The annual Spooky Art Show returns to Lavaun's Community Gallery for its third year, this time as “Skeleton's Out of the Closet.” Curated from an open call for submissions, this show features art that is spooky, scary, strange, and out of the ordinary. Alberta Street Gallery member Julia Alora, a lifetime lover of Halloween, has hand-picked this year’s collection of frights and delights from more than 10 local artists. What makes art spooky? Art that focuses on fears, phobias, or disquieting themes. Settings or characters or creatures that are dark, born from night, or upsetting to see. Images that capture the fun and nostalgia of playing in a scary space through a safe lens, reminiscent of horror movies and Halloweens past. Come in for a thrill and a chill, find a new piece to haunt your home, and enjoy beautiful works of art perfect for those who are strange and unusual. Alberta Street Gallery is a friendly and vibrant cooperative gallery of 30 local artists in the heart of the Alberta Arts District in Northeast Portland. In addition to our members’ art, we mount monthly shows that begin on the “Last Thursday” of every month. Our front windows feature new work by two of our member artists, and we curate group shows in Lavaun's Community Gallery, a special exhibition space inside the gallery named for and made possible by gallery member Lavaun Benavidez Heaster, a legally blind collage artist who died in 2020.

events.summary: Discover the history of the first Oregon Grange, organized in 1872, only five years after the National Grange was founded in Washington, D.C. The movement spread quickly when granges in the Midwest succeeded in lobbying for state legislatures to regulate rates charged by railroads and grain elevators, among other political wins. At its height, when Oregon had over 300 community granges with total membership up to 30,000, the State Grange had real influence in Salem. Historian Marilyn Reiher explains how the grange movement carries on serving the needs of its communities. Marilyn Reiher is author of Oregon State Grange: Serving Communities for 150 Years.
events.title: Oregon State Grange: Serving Communities for 150 Years

events.summary: Our Foundation series is geared towards students who are new to improvisation. This series welcomes people from all backgrounds, both creative and non-creative, so no acting or performing skills are ever required; just a desire to have fun, trust your instincts, and learn new ways to communicate and collaborate! Watch this 2min video from our Founder to learn more about what to expect from our classes: https://youtu.be/jbL1cooOIPA?si=WjHEZJoY7OZL05yd Our joyous & engaging classes are designed for anyone new to the practice of improvisation and for those wishing to re-learn or deepen their practice of the art form's basics. We'll learn about: 👂🏼New ways of listening 🎁 The gifts of staying in the moment 📚 Telling spontaneous stories with others 👣 Thinking on our feet & trusting our instincts 👥 Quickly collaborating with others 👀 Identifying & using non-verbal communication 💪🏼 Discovering our strengths Why Take Classes With Us? Our studio is founded on the belief that student progress only comes from providing clear instruction and feedback. We not only want our students to learn the core skills of improvisation, but we also want them to improve their skills over their time with us. Because of that, we offer learning opportunities that students won't find anywhere else. All of our students will receive the following: A safe, nurturing, and supportive environment 10 students max per class, so each gets lots of attention We offer flexible class options so students can purchase the number of classes that suits their schedule Coaching and check-ins during & after each game to help make sure you've understood the breakthroughs Blackboard discussions during class, when necessary, to help visual and analytical learners Closing every class with students recognising their own wins Receiving highly personalised notes via email from your teacher, celebrating your wins during the class series & recommending skills to work on when you come back for another class with us. Participating - for those who wish! - in our student showcases Receiving and reviewing vids & pics from our showcase as keepsakes and learning tools

events.summary: The Multnomah Arts Center (MAC) presents A Good Universe Next Door – A redacted past, a precarious present, and an uncertain future, a group exhibition curated by Celeste Noche and Melanie Stevens. On view in the Front & Center Galleries from September 18 through October 17, 2026, the exhibition features new work by four regional artists: Amber Capwell, Ebony Frison, Maryanna Hollomon, and Orlando Almanza. An opening reception will be held Saturday, September 19, from 1–3 p.m., and an artist talk will take place Saturday, October 10 at 2 p.m. Stevens and Noche invited the artists to consider how utopia and dystopia manifest in their lives, and how they interpret these experiences. Through sculpture, photography, printmaking, and painting, the artists offer visions of futures shaped by remembrance, resistance, solidarity, creativity, and care. Ebony Frison approaches utopia and dystopia as “conditions that coexist within the same historical moment.” Working with archival research, printmaking, photography, and artist books, Frison examines how Black histories persist despite erasure, describing utopia as “a practice of rememory—an active engagement with ancestral knowledge, community care, and historical reclamation.” Maryanna Hollomon highlights the aftermath of war for children and the global systems that produce displacement. “A utopia cannot be achieved without working in solidarity with those most oppressed,” she writes. Her work asks viewers to consider militarism’s impact and to imagine new forms of resistance and collective care. Amber Capwell creates sculptural works that envision utopian possibilities through Tarot readings for endangered Pacific Northwest flora and fauna. “These sculptures exist as a reminder to care,” they write. Their work incorporates queer and trans identities as part of an ecological futurism that demands “a utopia existing where we are allowed to live and thrive.” Orlando Almanza imagines futures built on safety, connection, and community. “I dream of a place where my people can have picnics next to the river, to rest, to laugh… and the grandmothers can enjoy their old age, sitting in their rocking chairs on their front porch,” he writes. “Sueño con el día que pueda ver a mi familia reunida, en la tierra que nos vio nacer” (I dream that one day my family can be reunited, in the land that birthed us). The Multnomah Arts Center is located at 7688 SW Capitol Hwy, Portland, OR, 97219. It is open Monday – Thursday 9 a.m. to 9:30 p.m., and Friday – Saturday 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. Additional Information: The Multnomah Arts Center is a part of Portland Parks & Recreation. MAC offers programs in a wide range of visual, music, movement, theater, and literary arts at an affordable cost to people of all ages. In addition to this vibrant arts education program, MAC runs a community-based visual arts exhibition program, which includes the MAC Front & Center Galleries. MAC also hosts theatre, music and dance performances, and other special events. The Multnomah Arts Center Association (MACA) is an all-volunteer, 501(c)(3) nonprofit organization that exists to support equity and access to arts education at MAC. MACA provides scholarships, supports community engagements efforts, and provides specialized arts equipment and facility improvements. Their efforts expand opportunities and enhance the experience of students, instructors, and the community at-large. For more information about MAC or MACA, please call 503.823.2787 or visit www.multnomahartscenter.org.
events.title: A Good Universe Next Door

events.summary: PDX CONTEMPORARY ART is pleased to present Soñé Que Revelabas, a solo exhibition of new work by photographer Georgina Reskala. The works in the exhibition center on a dream the artist had last year in which she approached her late sister, who whispered to her “Soñé que revelabas” or “I dreamed that you revealed.” Revelar in Spanish means to manifest or make public something that was secret or unknown, and is also the chemical process in photography by which a latent image becomes visible. She awoke trying to make sense of this message and wrote the sentence on a piece of paper on her studio wall. As the days and months went by, Reskala realized that she was still trying to make sense of the loss of her sister. Loss of language, interactions, moments, and memories that become fainter as a result of distance and time. This body of work became a personal account of the process of translation, not just in language, but of sounds, inflections, stories, memories, and dreams. Working with silver gelatin prints and photographs printed on textile, Reskala explores this estrangement that comes with the inability to fully translate from one language to another. Using a variety of printing techniques, she repeatedly alters her images, adding and redacting information through material processes of physically manipulating the paper, unthreading the warp and weft of the linen, and by printing, rephotographing, and reprinting the same image multiple times.
events.title: Georgina Reskala ·

events.summary: Curated by Harriet Tubman Center for Expanded Curatorial Practice at MLK School and Lisa Jarrett Drawing from the Museum’s collection, this exhibition is co-curated by Lisa Jarrett, an artist, educator, and curator, and the Harriet Tubman Center for Expanded Curatorial Practice at MLK Elementary— a group of 4th and 5th grade curators from KSMoCA. Working from a conversation with notable curators Dr. Lowery Stokes Sims and Dr. Leslie King Hammond, the exhibition engages PAM’s collection in new dialogues shaped by emerging curatorial voices and multigenerational knowledge. From theme and concept development, through work selection, and installation, this community curators project highlights the collaborative nature of curatorial practice and museum work. Harriet Tubman Center for Expanded Curatorial Practice at MLK School \(HTC\) is a KSMoCA project. Students participate directly in shaping exhibitions, positioning them as contributors to the museum, and engaging them as researchers, writers, planners, and curators. Through workshops and field trips, students collaborate with artists, visiting curators, and mentors from Portland State University’s College of the Arts. They research how exhibitions are developed, how artworks are interpreted, and how institutional decisions shape public understanding. Expanded curatorial practice includes visual art, writing, performance, research, publishing, and social practice. Co-founded by Lisa Jarrett and Harrell Fletcher, the project began in 2018 at Harriet Tubman Middle School and continues in its current iteration at Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. Elementary School.

events.summary: Inspired by Katherine Ace’s 9 Portraits as the foundational starting point for the exhibition, Nine Women Artists will feature the work of the artists shown in Ace’s portrait painting. All mature artists in their careers and with a significant presence in the Northwest, their work reveals a diverse expression of artistic styles from representation to abstraction. There are rich details in the painting. Most notably on the left hangs Henri Fantin-Latour’s A Studio at Les Batignolles, 1870 \(Musée d’Orsay\). In this painting is a formal gathering of male artists. In response to this painting, Katherine asked her subjects to dress in their studio/work clothes as counterpoint, all marked in their characteristic poses. Other Portland women artists are recognized here through their paintings—a small Sally Haley still life hangs in the background, as well as an Amanda Snyder painting behind Phyllis Yes. And to the far right, we have a glimpse of Lucinda Parker’s very large work. Postcards and newspapers scattered on the floor are the exhibition announcements and reviews highlighting the artists’ works. An epic portrait featuring nine women artists of the Northwest, Ace responded to the lack of self-portraits by women artists in history. From left, the artists are: Laura Ross-Paul, Katherine’s self-portrait seated with phone, Mary Josephson, Judy Cooke, Phyllis Yes, Sharon Bronzan, Shu-Ju Wang, Lucinda Parker, and Sherrie Wolf. All are women artists who have made long careers in Portland. As Ace notes about these women, “They have tenacity, have lived through sexist decades, told they couldn’t really be artists—only fit for sleeping with the professor, expected to subvert themselves to male artist machismo.”
events.title: Nine Women Artists

events.summary: Skeletons Out of the Closet The annual Spooky Art Show returns to Lavaun's Community Gallery for its third year, this time as “Skeleton's Out of the Closet.” Curated from an open call for submissions, this show features art that is spooky, scary, strange, and out of the ordinary. Alberta Street Gallery member Julia Alora, a lifetime lover of Halloween, has hand-picked this year’s collection of frights and delights from more than 10 local artists. What makes art spooky? Art that focuses on fears, phobias, or disquieting themes. Settings or characters or creatures that are dark, born from night, or upsetting to see. Images that capture the fun and nostalgia of playing in a scary space through a safe lens, reminiscent of horror movies and Halloweens past. Come in for a thrill and a chill, find a new piece to haunt your home, and enjoy beautiful works of art perfect for those who are strange and unusual. Alberta Street Gallery is a friendly and vibrant cooperative gallery of 30 local artists in the heart of the Alberta Arts District in Northeast Portland. In addition to our members’ art, we mount monthly shows that begin on the “Last Thursday” of every month. Our front windows feature new work by two of our member artists, and we curate group shows in Lavaun's Community Gallery, a special exhibition space inside the gallery named for and made possible by gallery member Lavaun Benavidez Heaster, a legally blind collage artist who died in 2020.
events.title: Skeletons Out of the Closet: A Spooky Art Show

events.summary: Description Join us for this informational session on our Trip to Costa Rica!! Beaverton Area Chamber of Commerce presents Tropical Costa Rica! Discover Costa Rica's pura vida on a rendezvous with exotic fauna, lush rainforests, and endless coastlines. Beaverton Area Chamber of Commerce is pleased to announce a new travel program available to the entire community. Working in alliance with chamber member Gold Keys Travel and Collette, an award-winning guided tour operator, our greater community will be able to experience expertly curated tours that connect travelers to the world's iconic sights, culture, and local people of a destination. Join us for a trip of a lifetime, July 11- 27, 2027, as we explore the magic of Costa Rica! Gain inspiration through other people and cultures, experience some of the most awe-inspiring settings on earth, and support the Beaverton Area Chamber of Commerce and its mission to promote a vibrant community through a network of chamber member businesses, non-members, and tourism alliances. About This Tour Lush forests and stunning waterfalls… rumbling volcanoes and endless coastlines… Costa Rica is a paradise teeming with exotic plants and incredible animals. Enjoy the tranquil views of Arenal Volcano from your hotel. Explore part of the 20,000-acre nature preserve of Cano Negro on a riverboat adventure. Spend two nights in Monteverde's lush cloud forest. Experience the forest canopy on your choice of a hanging bridges nature walk or an exhilarating zip lining tour. Soak in the sunshine at Playa Carrillo, Guanacaste, known for its breathtaking beauty and fine sandy beaches. You will find a slice of paradise and so much more. Must-See Inclusions Spot indigenous wildlife while on a Cano Negro riverboat cruise. Enjoy the breathtaking scenery surrounding Arenal Volcano. Put your feet up and relax during a 2-night stay in Guanacaste known for the country's most beautiful beaches. Cultural Connections Catch a glimpse of local life as you explore a family-owned farm. Join an engaging talk led by a local birding expert, exploring the fascinating migration patterns of the county's avian visitors. Culinary Inclusions Discover the history of coffee in Costa Rica during your visit to a coffee plantation. Enjoy a farm-to-table lunch featuring fresh organic ingredients and traditional Costa Rican flavors.

events.summary: Literary Arts is excited to welcome author and journalist Ali Francis to celebrate her debut book, The Curious Lives of Vegetables, a wild journey through the hidden histories of plants. Francis will be joined by Portland writers Lola Milholland \(Group Living and Other Recipes\) and Andrew Barton \(Free Food: earth eating, The Long Loaf, The Myrtlewood Cookbook\) for a conversation moderated by environmental journalist and author Devon Fredericksen \(How to Camp in the Woods\). Together, they’ll explore what food can tell us about how we live: our relationships with plants and place, the ways knowledge and traditions move between people, what gets lost when food systems become less diverse, and what we might recover by paying closer attention to the things we eat. Moving from vegetables and biodiversity to bread, communal tables, regional foodways, and the everyday work of feeding people, the conversation will consider food not simply as something we consume, but as a reflection of our relationships with the natural world. About the book: Why are some carrots purple? What does a 1,000-year-old lotus seed have to tell us about survival? How did a tomato named for Paul Robeson become a political symbol? And what disappears when a vegetable disappears? In The Curious Lives of Vegetables, Australian journalist Ali Francis goes digging into the astonishing stories hiding in our crisper drawers, gardens, markets, and seed banks. Across more than 100 beautifully illustrated stories, she traces the plants we eat through migration and colonialism, politics and religion, extinction and revival, revealing vegetables as living records of human history — and essential seeds for a more resilient future. Along the way, Francis encounters ancient seeds brought back from the dead, vegetables carried across borders by displaced communities, plants transformed by centuries of human preference, and varieties now teetering on the edge of extinction. At once playful, deeply researched, and urgent, The Curious Lives of Vegetables asks us to look again at the ordinary plants on our plates, and to consider their extraordinary importance.
events.title: Andrew Barton, Ali Francis, and Lola Milholland in conversation

events.summary: Kelsey Lu is a classically trained cellist, singer-songwriter, producer, composer, poet, and performance artist born in Charlotte, North Carolina, whose practice flows at the intersection of visual art, performance, healing, and music. From her striking 2016 EP Church to groundbreaking 2019 debut album 'Blood,' Lu collaborates with artists across disciplines, including Lady Gaga, Kim Gordon, Yves Tumor, Sampha, Florence \+ The Machine, Skrillex, Kahlil Joseph, Wu Tsang, Precious Okoyomon, and Jacolby Satterwhite. Lu's recent projects include scoring the award-winning documentary 'DAUGHTERS' \(Netflix/XTR\), Savanah Leaf's BAFTA-winning 'Earth Mama' \(A24\), and starring in and scoring Janicza Bravo's 'House Comes With a Bird' alongside Pedro Pascal and Natasha Lyonne. Other notable works include the Guggenheim-commissioned installation Anthem with Beverly Glenn-Copeland, a sound piece for the 2022 Venice Biennale with Sophia Al-Maria, performances at the Metropolitan Museum of Art, starring in Gucci's 2024 blondie bag campaign shot by Nan Goldin, and starring in and scoring campaigns for various fashion labels such as Chanel, Jil Sander, and Miu Miu. With new music arriving this year and a second album coming next year, Lu continues expanding the boundaries of artistic expression.
events.title: Kelsey Lu

events.summary: Volunteer with us! We're celebrating the end of the volunteer season at Laurelhurst Park. Join us for our final work party of 2026 as we get the plants ready for fall and winter! As usual, new and returning volunteers are welcome to attend drop-in style, and no previous gardening experience is required to participate. This is a great opportunity to learn more about gardening, plants, and to connect with your neighbors and community. Plant care activities vary monthly. Tools and instructions provided. Open to all skills, paces, and abilities. We'll also have plenty of snacks, treats, and pizza as an offering of appreciation to everyone who has helped us care for the park this year. Gluten-free and vegan options included. Participants 16 and younger should be accompanied by a parent or responsible adult. Meet at the green PP&R building on the north side of the park, 3600 SE Ankeny St. Contact the Friends of Laurelhurst Park Portland Parks & Recreation works in partnership with the Friends of Laurelhurst Park to help maintain and sustain the flora in the park. Together, we host monthly volunteer events from April through October. The Friends of Laurelhurst Park are seeking new volunteers to help with organizing and leadership in the group! This is a great opportunity to get more involved in tending the park. For questions about volunteering at a monthly work party or if you are interested in learning more about volunteering with FLP in a leadership capacity, please contact the Friends of Laurelhurst Park at laurelhurst.parkfriends@gmail.com . Event Reminders Inclement Weather Plan: We usually work rain, shine, and in between! Volunteer events will be cancelled due to inclement and severe weather. Please bring a reusable water bottle if you have one, and any snacks you may need. Wear sturdy close-toed shoes, clothes you don't mind getting a little dirty, and layers to dress for the weather. Work looks and feels different for every body. We encourage volunteers to go at their own pace and take breaks to rest. Keep yourself and your community safe and healthy - please stay home if you are sick. There will always be more opportunities to volunteer with us! To find bus routes and public transportation options, check out the TriMet Trip Planner tool . Looking for community service to fulfill court requirements? Please call 503-823-5121 or contact the event coordinator listed on this page. You must be registered with the program before participating in any community service. Site Accessibility Laurelhurst Park is a large site with paved pathways throughout the park. There are many different parts of the park we will work in during monthly volunteer events. Some activities may require bending, kneeling, stooping, or navigating across grass or up and down inclines. Many parts of the park are heavily shaded, with some areas having open sun exposure. There are ADA accessible restrooms on-site. If you have an ADA accommodation request to be able to participate in this volunteer event, please use the 311 ADA Accommodation Request webpage . If you would like to learn more about or request language access services, please contact PDX 311 . We recommend making your request as soon as possible and at least 5 business days \(Monday - Friday\) in advance of the event. If you have questions about the accessibility of the event, please contact Developed Parks Coordinator, Kimberléa Ruffu \(they/them\) at kimberlea.ruffu@portlandoregon.gov .
events.title: End of Season Celebration! Laurelhurst Park Community Volunteer Day

events.summary: The Multnomah Arts Center (MAC) presents A Good Universe Next Door – A redacted past, a precarious present, and an uncertain future, a group exhibition curated by Celeste Noche and Melanie Stevens. On view in the Front & Center Galleries from September 18 through October 17, 2026, the exhibition features new work by four regional artists: Amber Capwell, Ebony Frison, Maryanna Hollomon, and Orlando Almanza. An opening reception will be held Saturday, September 19, from 1–3 p.m., and an artist talk will take place Saturday, October 10 at 2 p.m. Stevens and Noche invited the artists to consider how utopia and dystopia manifest in their lives, and how they interpret these experiences. Through sculpture, photography, printmaking, and painting, the artists offer visions of futures shaped by remembrance, resistance, solidarity, creativity, and care. Ebony Frison approaches utopia and dystopia as “conditions that coexist within the same historical moment.” Working with archival research, printmaking, photography, and artist books, Frison examines how Black histories persist despite erasure, describing utopia as “a practice of rememory—an active engagement with ancestral knowledge, community care, and historical reclamation.” Maryanna Hollomon highlights the aftermath of war for children and the global systems that produce displacement. “A utopia cannot be achieved without working in solidarity with those most oppressed,” she writes. Her work asks viewers to consider militarism’s impact and to imagine new forms of resistance and collective care. Amber Capwell creates sculptural works that envision utopian possibilities through Tarot readings for endangered Pacific Northwest flora and fauna. “These sculptures exist as a reminder to care,” they write. Their work incorporates queer and trans identities as part of an ecological futurism that demands “a utopia existing where we are allowed to live and thrive.” Orlando Almanza imagines futures built on safety, connection, and community. “I dream of a place where my people can have picnics next to the river, to rest, to laugh… and the grandmothers can enjoy their old age, sitting in their rocking chairs on their front porch,” he writes. “Sueño con el día que pueda ver a mi familia reunida, en la tierra que nos vio nacer” (I dream that one day my family can be reunited, in the land that birthed us). The Multnomah Arts Center is located at 7688 SW Capitol Hwy, Portland, OR, 97219. It is open Monday – Thursday 9 a.m. to 9:30 p.m., and Friday – Saturday 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. Additional Information: The Multnomah Arts Center is a part of Portland Parks & Recreation. MAC offers programs in a wide range of visual, music, movement, theater, and literary arts at an affordable cost to people of all ages. In addition to this vibrant arts education program, MAC runs a community-based visual arts exhibition program, which includes the MAC Front & Center Galleries. MAC also hosts theatre, music and dance performances, and other special events. The Multnomah Arts Center Association (MACA) is an all-volunteer, 501(c)(3) nonprofit organization that exists to support equity and access to arts education at MAC. MACA provides scholarships, supports community engagements efforts, and provides specialized arts equipment and facility improvements. Their efforts expand opportunities and enhance the experience of students, instructors, and the community at-large. For more information about MAC or MACA, please call 503.823.2787 or visit www.multnomahartscenter.org.
events.title: A Good Universe Next Door

events.summary: PDX CONTEMPORARY ART is pleased to present Soñé Que Revelabas, a solo exhibition of new work by photographer Georgina Reskala. The works in the exhibition center on a dream the artist had last year in which she approached her late sister, who whispered to her “Soñé que revelabas” or “I dreamed that you revealed.” Revelar in Spanish means to manifest or make public something that was secret or unknown, and is also the chemical process in photography by which a latent image becomes visible. She awoke trying to make sense of this message and wrote the sentence on a piece of paper on her studio wall. As the days and months went by, Reskala realized that she was still trying to make sense of the loss of her sister. Loss of language, interactions, moments, and memories that become fainter as a result of distance and time. This body of work became a personal account of the process of translation, not just in language, but of sounds, inflections, stories, memories, and dreams. Working with silver gelatin prints and photographs printed on textile, Reskala explores this estrangement that comes with the inability to fully translate from one language to another. Using a variety of printing techniques, she repeatedly alters her images, adding and redacting information through material processes of physically manipulating the paper, unthreading the warp and weft of the linen, and by printing, rephotographing, and reprinting the same image multiple times.
events.title: Georgina Reskala ·

events.summary: Lookout Landscape is an immersive art exhibition by Oregon-based artist and designer David Buckley Borden and a team of collaborators working across forestry, design, and engineering. Inspired by fire lookout towers, trail culture, and backcountry gear, the exhibition invites visitors onto a fabricated “Lookout Trail,” where a series of imaginative scenes—from a trailhead to a weather station, campground, and tool shed—reimagine the visual language of forestry and outdoor culture in the Pacific Northwest. Blending research, humor, and design, the exhibition explores the complex relationships between people and working forests, with wildfire as an underlying thread. As visitors move through the space, they are encouraged to reflect on how forests are shaped, valued, and cared for, and to consider their own connection to these landscapes. Plan your visit and explore the exhibition: worldforestry.org/lookout-landscape

events.summary: This former Southern Pacific Railroad station, fondly called the Old Train Station \(OTS\), is home to Friends of Historic Forest Grove. The Old Train Station now serves as a museum highlighting about 150 years of local history, from photographs and maps to clothing and furniture. It also houses an historic library and research center. Built in 1913, the station handled passenger and light freight service into 1929. After that only light freight came through. Burlingham and Sons purchased the building as office space for their seed company. Unfortunately, over the years this building has gone through some internal and external changes but some of the original station remains and can easy be found. Woodfold acquired the building from Burlingham and has graciously allowed Friends to use the building since 2008. Please stop by and see what we have to offer. Check website to confirm open hours

events.summary: Curated by Harriet Tubman Center for Expanded Curatorial Practice at MLK School and Lisa Jarrett Drawing from the Museum’s collection, this exhibition is co-curated by Lisa Jarrett, an artist, educator, and curator, and the Harriet Tubman Center for Expanded Curatorial Practice at MLK Elementary— a group of 4th and 5th grade curators from KSMoCA. Working from a conversation with notable curators Dr. Lowery Stokes Sims and Dr. Leslie King Hammond, the exhibition engages PAM’s collection in new dialogues shaped by emerging curatorial voices and multigenerational knowledge. From theme and concept development, through work selection, and installation, this community curators project highlights the collaborative nature of curatorial practice and museum work. Harriet Tubman Center for Expanded Curatorial Practice at MLK School \(HTC\) is a KSMoCA project. Students participate directly in shaping exhibitions, positioning them as contributors to the museum, and engaging them as researchers, writers, planners, and curators. Through workshops and field trips, students collaborate with artists, visiting curators, and mentors from Portland State University’s College of the Arts. They research how exhibitions are developed, how artworks are interpreted, and how institutional decisions shape public understanding. Expanded curatorial practice includes visual art, writing, performance, research, publishing, and social practice. Co-founded by Lisa Jarrett and Harrell Fletcher, the project began in 2018 at Harriet Tubman Middle School and continues in its current iteration at Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. Elementary School.
events.title: Harriet Tubman Center Museum

events.summary: Inspired by Katherine Ace’s 9 Portraits as the foundational starting point for the exhibition, Nine Women Artists will feature the work of the artists shown in Ace’s portrait painting. All mature artists in their careers and with a significant presence in the Northwest, their work reveals a diverse expression of artistic styles from representation to abstraction. There are rich details in the painting. Most notably on the left hangs Henri Fantin-Latour’s A Studio at Les Batignolles, 1870 \(Musée d’Orsay\). In this painting is a formal gathering of male artists. In response to this painting, Katherine asked her subjects to dress in their studio/work clothes as counterpoint, all marked in their characteristic poses. Other Portland women artists are recognized here through their paintings—a small Sally Haley still life hangs in the background, as well as an Amanda Snyder painting behind Phyllis Yes. And to the far right, we have a glimpse of Lucinda Parker’s very large work. Postcards and newspapers scattered on the floor are the exhibition announcements and reviews highlighting the artists’ works. An epic portrait featuring nine women artists of the Northwest, Ace responded to the lack of self-portraits by women artists in history. From left, the artists are: Laura Ross-Paul, Katherine’s self-portrait seated with phone, Mary Josephson, Judy Cooke, Phyllis Yes, Sharon Bronzan, Shu-Ju Wang, Lucinda Parker, and Sherrie Wolf. All are women artists who have made long careers in Portland. As Ace notes about these women, “They have tenacity, have lived through sexist decades, told they couldn’t really be artists—only fit for sleeping with the professor, expected to subvert themselves to male artist machismo.”
events.title: Nine Women Artists

events.summary: Chefas Projects is pleased to present Galvanized, the first solo exhibition at the gallery by Portland artist Bobby Adams. On view September 18 through October 17, the exhibition brings together seven new gradient paintings that extend Adams’s ongoing investigation into color, movement, precision, and reduction. Working with hard edges and meticulously calibrated color transitions, Adams constructs paintings that appear at once exacting and elusive. Color becomes both subject and structure: gradients shift across the surface with a measured sense of movement, while simplified compositions heighten the perceptual effects of scale, saturation, and transition. The paintings inhabit a productive space between the mechanical and the handmade, where precision does not eliminate the presence of the artist but makes it more apparent. Adams’s approach is informed by a background outside of traditional art-making. Before turning to painting in 2017, he worked in product development and ran a clothing line for eight years. That experience with materials, systems, color, and visual identity remains embedded in his practice. His paintings share an affinity with the economy and immediacy of graphic design while resisting its fixedness; seemingly simple arrangements become dynamic through subtle shifts in color and proportion. The title Galvanized gestures toward a central tension within the work: the desire to achieve a polished, controlled image alongside the inevitable irregularities of its making. Adams’s paintings are rigorously constructed, but they are not anonymous. Their surfaces hold the evidence of decisions, adjustments, and the physical act of painting. Running through the exhibition is Adams’s longstanding relationship to NASCAR, a significant influence on his upbringing and visual sensibility. The sport’s saturated palettes, speed, spectacle, and graphic intensity provide an unexpected point of departure for paintings that are otherwise characterized by restraint. In California Poppy, this connection is particularly pronounced. Its color relationships carry the visual charge of racing culture while being distilled through Adams’s pared-down formal language. The result is a body of work in which speed is suggested rather than depicted, and where movement emerges from the most economical means. Adams takes visual cues associated with motion, competition, and spectacle and subjects them to the slower, more deliberate logic of abstraction. Galvanized marks an important step in Adams’s relationship with the gallery, following his inclusion in multiple group exhibitions and establishing a sustained presentation of his practice through a focused body of new work.
events.title: BOBBY ADAMS | GALVANIZED

events.summary: Chefas Projects is pleased to present Mercurial, a new solo exhibition by sculptural artist Dan Lam, on view September 18 through October 17, 2026. Bringing together more than twenty new works, the exhibition introduces a heightened metallic sensibility to Lam’s singular sculptural language, with surfaces that suggest chrome, liquid metal, and something less readily identifiable-objects caught somewhere between matter and mutation. Known for sculptures that occupy an uncanny space between the organic and the artificial, Lam approaches form as something fluid, seductive, and alive. In Mercurial, this sensibility takes on a distinctly reflective character. Metallic hues course across the surfaces of the works, emphasizing their bulbous contours, dripping edges, and seemingly unstable forms. Chrome-like finishes catch and distort their surroundings, allowing the sculptures to shift with changes in light, perspective, and proximity. The works appear to ooze, pool, drip, and swell. Their surfaces suggest viscosity while their forms remain resolutely sculptural, creating an intriguing contradiction between solidity and liquidity. They seem less like objects that have been made than organisms in the midst of becoming - alien, tactile, and strangely familiar. This tension is fundamental to Lam’s practice. Her sculptures consistently operate between opposing states: attraction and repulsion, organic and inanimate, soft and hard, seriousness and play. Rather than resolving these contradictions, Lam uses them as points of departure. The resulting forms possess an uncanny immediacy, inviting viewers to move closer even as their unfamiliarity introduces a note of hesitation. In Mercurial, the reflective surfaces intensify this exchange between object and viewer. The sculptures absorb fragments of their environments and return them altered, making the surrounding space part of the work. What initially reads as an autonomous object becomes something more relational-a form that changes depending on where it is encountered and how it is seen. Despite their otherworldly appearance, Lam’s sculptures remain remarkably approachable. Playfulness is central to their charge. The works resist the distance sometimes associated with contemporary sculpture, instead engaging the viewer through color, surface, scale, and a visceral sense of recognition. They are strange without being alienating; experimental without abandoning the pleasures of looking. The title Mercurial evokes both the mutable nature of the works and their affinity with mercury: a substance defined by its fluidity, reflectivity, and ability to transform its appearance in relation to its surroundings. Here, Lam translates those qualities into sculptural form. Her objects appear perpetually in motion, suspended between states, as though their final form has not yet been decided. Across more than twenty new sculptures, Mercurial expands Lam’s investigation of the space between the familiar and the unknown. The works activate the imagination through an intuitive visual language - one based not on representation but on sensation. Their exaggerated forms, seductive surfaces, and ambiguous materiality encourage viewers to project, imagine, and participate. In Lam’s hands, sculpture becomes less a fixed thing than an encounter: part organism, part object, part fantasy. Mercurial embraces that instability, presenting a body of work that is at once polished and unruly, seductive and strange, playful and profound.

events.summary: The spiral holds great meaning for cultures all over the world and has captivated our attention throughout ancient and modern time. Whether of metaphysical and philosophical significance, or the many scientific and biological iterations of this powerful symbol, the multi-faceted spiral will be our muse. In this 3-part generative writing workshop, we’ll expand our writing across multiple genres including poetry, essay, and narrative with prompts inspired by multicultural authors. Thematically, we’ll move through Irish-Celtic mysticism, spiraling seasons of emergence, Afro-futurist science fiction, and our personal place within the great spiral. We’ll engage impactful elements of style and craft from our mentor texts like punctuation, dialogue, and symbol to enhance writing of resonance. Some time will be devoted to giving and receiving feedback as well as sharing in a supportive space. Writers of all levels and backgrounds are welcome. Course Outcomes Writers will: Explore a variety of multicultural texts as inspiration for writing. Draft poems, creative non-fiction, and narrative pieces related to spirals. Engage elements of craft and style from multigenre model texts. Enhance writing through feedback and sharing in positive and supportive circles. Access Program We want our writing classes and seminars to be accessible to everyone, regardless of income and background. We understand that our tuition structure can present obstacles for some people. Our Access Program offers writing class and seminar tuitions at a reduced rate. Most writing classes have at least one access spot available. Please apply here for access rate tuition. Contact Susan Moore at susan@literary-arts.org if you have questions. Liaison position Every in-person class and seminar at Literary Arts has one liaison position. Liaisons perform specific duties for each class meeting. If you are a liaison for a class or seminar, the full amount of your tuition is covered by Literary Arts. Apply here for the liaison position.
events.title: Writing Spirals: Multicultural Contemplations on Beginnings, Endings, and Cycles

events.summary: As Oregonians celebrate the 100th anniversary of Highway 101, the New Deal bridges that completed this iconic highway are celebrating their 90th anniversary. In 1934, construction began on the five bridges designed to close the remaining watery gaps on Oregon's Highway 101. By the summer of 1936, New Deal funding assisted in completing bridges across the five widest bays and estuaries at Newport, Reedsport, Waldport, Florence, and Coos Bay. Robert W. Hadlow and Judith Kenny explore the significance of these bridges as Depression-era projects, examples of the state bridge engineer Conde B. McCullough's design excellence, and their importance carrying us into the 21st century. Judith Kenny is the director of the Oregon Chapter of the Living New Deal, and Robert W. Hadlow is the author of Elegant Arches, Soaring Spans: C.B. McCullough, Oregon's Master Bridge Builder.
events.title: History Pub - The New Deal Bridges of the Oregon Coast

Through song, dance, and short theatrical vignettes, the altar gradually takes shape as an act of remembrance and cultural inheritance, inviting audiences to consider how traditions are taught, how memory is kept alive, and what is carried forward when we share rituals across generations. events.summary: Amélie Farren started writing songs at twelve because she needed somewhere to put things. That hasn't changed. At 18, she writes alt-folk/alt-pop songs specific enough to make a listener feel like they're inside a moment they know well but never had words for. Her debut release suffering has passed 24 million streams. Unsweetened Lemonade \(2024\) followed with over 70 million, finding listeners across the US, UK, Europe, Asia and South America through songs that people kept coming back to. Her debut album Airheaded, produced by Michael Keenan in LA, is a collection of songs about obsession, complicated attachment, and the odd parallels between the person causing harm and the person on the receiving end. In May 2026 she has a new EP, Infanescence. Where Airheaded was about what people do to each other, Infanescence is about what time does to a person. It sits in that gap between still feeling like a kid and knowing you're not one anymore. -- Lilith Max is a master of storytelling, weaving tales of enchantment and whimsy. Her fantasy-folk-inspired music pulls the audience into a world of knights, myths, and magic, giving listeners room for their imagination to roam free. Originally from northern Germany and living in the U.S., Lilith began diving into the world of myth and folktale early on. German stories like the Erl King \(Erl König\) and fairytales like Rumpelstiltskin sparked her curiosity, so she incorporated their magic into her music. Through alluring melodies, Lilith also highlights the deeper meanings in her work. In tracks like “Circe”, “Peasant’s Throne”, and “Call Down The Dragon”, the artist addresses topics of female rage, social pressure, climate change, inner struggle, and more. With catchy rhythms and deep lyrics, Lilith creates layers of enjoyment for those who wish to dance along and those who wish to hear her powerful words. Having spent much of her teenage years in the acting industry of Hollywood, Lilith integrates cinematic drama into her stage and online presence. Fans know Lilith Max for her unique music skits and the soul-piercing expressions she casts at the camera. On stage, Lilith becomes a whirlwind of dancing and twirling, evolving her performance with every shift of the music. Lilith Max’s exceptional vocal range and vocal control are a hallmark of her music. She fills the air with angelic high notes and pulls the audience into the depths of her low timbre. -- Rabbitology is the project of Nat Timmerman—a world that was pulled from her odd-running mind. A little land of the harebrained and burrowing. Simply follow the three-legged rabbit prints until you’re knee deep in this world’s eclectic soundscapes, and here you will discover a collection of memoirs turned into fantastical sonic short stories. Stay as long as you like. Make this world your home too. It’s a little unusual in here, but that’s life!

events.summary: Each week, we will read and discuss short pieces and excerpts from contemporary authors who are known to weave their pasts into the present including Annie Erneaux, Joan Didion, Ayad Aktar, Sonya Walger, Aysegul Savas, Rachel Cusk, Emmanuel Carrere, and others. There were also be to weekly craft essays on various genres \(memoir, personal essay, autofiction and hybrid\). There will be an opportunity to submit one short excerpt of your own writing within this framework \(can be from a short story, a personal essay or a novel-in-progress\) to be workshopped during the class. This course is generative, so participants should plan to write at least 1500 words per week. Most importantly, the goal of this course is to be inspired and to feel supported in your writing. This course is for all levels of writers and readers. Class assignments: Excerpts: Frances will provide two short \(10-15pp\) readings per week, excerpted from novels, memoirs, and stand-alone personal essay, to be discussed during the first part of class Craft essays: two craft essays/interviews, mostly in relation to the authors and genres discussed for the week, will be provided for discussion during the first part of class We will workshop two writers’ work per week after the first introductory class; participants should plan to submit 1500 words per week even if you are not being workshopped. Class outcomes: • exposure to contemporary writers who blend their past with the present day, namely personal essay, memoir and hybrid forms/autofiction • inspiring community dialogue and critique of contemporary authors • opportunity to workshop your writing and get constructive feedback • looking at your work through a bigger picture lens; where you see yourself in the literary landscape • writing practice/planning: during the first class and last class, we will discuss overall goals for your work, whether you want to complete a short story or a personal essay, plan a bigger project like a story collection, essay collection, memoir or novel/novella, or to simply establish a more consistent writing practice. Access Program We want our writing classes and seminars to be accessible to everyone, regardless of income and background. We understand that our tuition structure can present obstacles for some people. Our Access Program offers writing class and seminar tuitions at a reduced rate. events.summary: The Multnomah Arts Center (MAC) presents A Good Universe Next Door – A redacted past, a precarious present, and an uncertain future, a group exhibition curated by Celeste Noche and Melanie Stevens. On view in the Front & Center Galleries from September 18 through October 17, 2026, the exhibition features new work by four regional artists: Amber Capwell, Ebony Frison, Maryanna Hollomon, and Orlando Almanza. An opening reception will be held Saturday, September 19, from 1–3 p.m., and an artist talk will take place Saturday, October 10 at 2 p.m. Stevens and Noche invited the artists to consider how utopia and dystopia manifest in their lives, and how they interpret these experiences. Through sculpture, photography, printmaking, and painting, the artists offer visions of futures shaped by remembrance, resistance, solidarity, creativity, and care. Ebony Frison approaches utopia and dystopia as “conditions that coexist within the same historical moment.” Working with archival research, printmaking, photography, and artist books, Frison examines how Black histories persist despite erasure, describing utopia as “a practice of rememory—an active engagement with ancestral knowledge, community care, and historical reclamation.” Maryanna Hollomon highlights the aftermath of war for children and the global systems that produce displacement. “A utopia cannot be achieved without working in solidarity with those most oppressed,” she writes. Her work asks viewers to consider militarism’s impact and to imagine new forms of resistance and collective care. Amber Capwell creates sculptural works that envision utopian possibilities through Tarot readings for endangered Pacific Northwest flora and fauna. “These sculptures exist as a reminder to care,” they write. Their work incorporates queer and trans identities as part of an ecological futurism that demands “a utopia existing where we are allowed to live and thrive.” Orlando Almanza imagines futures built on safety, connection, and community. “I dream of a place where my people can have picnics next to the river, to rest, to laugh… and the grandmothers can enjoy their old age, sitting in their rocking chairs on their front porch,” he writes. “Sueño con el día que pueda ver a mi familia reunida, en la tierra que nos vio nacer” (I dream that one day my family can be reunited, in the land that birthed us). The Multnomah Arts Center is located at 7688 SW Capitol Hwy, Portland, OR, 97219. It is open Monday – Thursday 9 a.m. to 9:30 p.m., and Friday – Saturday 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. Additional Information: The Multnomah Arts Center is a part of Portland Parks & Recreation. MAC offers programs in a wide range of visual, music, movement, theater, and literary arts at an affordable cost to people of all ages. In addition to this vibrant arts education program, MAC runs a community-based visual arts exhibition program, which includes the MAC Front & Center Galleries. MAC also hosts theatre, music and dance performances, and other special events. The Multnomah Arts Center Association (MACA) is an all-volunteer, 501(c)(3) nonprofit organization that exists to support equity and access to arts education at MAC. MACA provides scholarships, supports community engagements efforts, and provides specialized arts equipment and facility improvements. Their efforts expand opportunities and enhance the experience of students, instructors, and the community at-large. For more information about MAC or MACA, please call 503.823.2787 or visit www.multnomahartscenter.org.
